opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy told Elizabeth that he had struggled in vain and that it would not do. His feelings would not be repressed, and he must allow him to tell her how ardently he admired and loved her.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth replied to Mr. Darcy that in such cases, it was believed to be the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It was natural that obligation should be felt, and if she could feel gratitude, she would now thank him. But she could not, for she had never desired his good opinion, and he had certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. She was sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone, but it had been most unconsciously done and she hoped it would be of short duration. The feelings which he told her had long prevented the acknowledgment of his regard could have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy told Elizabeth that this was all the reply which he was to have the honour of expecting. He might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, he was thus rejected. But it was of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth told Mr. Darcy that she might as well ask why, with such a clear intention of offending and insulting her, he chose to tell her that he liked her against his will, against his reason, and even against his character. Was not this some excuse for incivility, if she was uncivil? But she had other provocations. He knew she had. Had not her own feelings decided against him, had they been indifferent, or even favourable, did he think that any consideration would tempt her to accept the man who had been the means of ruining, perhaps forever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth told Mr. Darcy that she had every reason in the world to think ill of him. No motive could excuse the unjust and ungenerous part he had acted there. He dared not, he could not deny that he had been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth told Mr. Darcy that it was not merely this affair on which her dislike was founded. Long before it had taken place, her opinion of him was decided. His character was unfolded in the recital which she had received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what could he have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship could he here defend himself? Or under what misrepresentation could he here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: Mr. Darcy told Elizabeth that she took an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Elizabeth replied to Mr. Darcy that who that knew what his misfortunes had been could help feeling an interest in him?
